video_title: A World Model of Life: Biohub's Alex Rives on Virtual Cells, Measurement, & the $1.8B Data Push
gist: Biohub head of science Alex Rives (ex-EvolutionaryScale/ESM) argues current virtual cell models fall short mainly because biology is measurement-limited, and explains how Biohub's $1.8B Virtual Biology Initiative with DOE, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta, plus tools like the laser phase plate, aims to generate data for an information-theoretic cell model within ~5 years. He maps the LLM recipe (pre-training, elicitation, lab-verified RLVR) onto biology and stresses cross-species transfer over EHR-style correlation.

themes.theme: Why virtual cells don't work yet

insights.claim: Alex Rives of Biohub argues today's so-called virtual cell models do not meet the bar of a model that can meaningfully simulate the cell or serve as an oracle for experimental biology.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Discount claims from AI-bio startups marketing 'virtual cells' as drug-discovery oracles; the field is earlier than the hype suggests.
insights.quote: I don't think they meet that that definition of a model that that could actually simulate the cell in a meaningful way and actually really serve as an oracle for experimental biology

insights.claim: Rives frames solving cell modeling as requiring simultaneous progress on three fronts: modeling paradigms, data generation at scale, and measurement/observation tools that capture what actually matters in the cell.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Useful screen for AI-bio companies: those with only a model and no proprietary data or measurement edge are missing two of three legs.

insights.claim: Rives says the most fundamental bottleneck in cell modeling is observability and measurement — much of what happens in the cell cannot be measured at all, and much else cannot be measured at scale.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Value in AI-bio may accrue to measurement/instrumentation and data-generation platforms (imaging, spatial, single-cell) rather than to model builders alone.

insights.claim: Rives argues the standard transformer lacks the multi-scale structure needed to represent biology's levels of complexity from atoms to molecules to cells to tissues, leaving the right modeling paradigm an open question.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Room for new architectures in bio-AI; watch for multi-scale model announcements as a differentiator.

insights.claim: Rives contends that in the limit of infinite data and compute all model architectures converge as function approximators, but cellular biology is very far from that limit, so inductive bias matters a great deal — unlike protein biology, where sequencing at scale gets closer to the data limit.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Explains why protein models (ESM, AlphaFold) succeeded first and why cell-level models need domain-specific architectures or much more data.

insights.claim: Biology differs from other AI domains chiefly in the limits on our ability to observe and measure, and Rives notes many historic paradigm shifts in science came from new measurement technologies.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Supports investing in enabling-tool companies (microscopy, sequencing, spatial omics) as picks-and-shovels for the AI-bio wave.
insights.quote: I think the biggest difference is the the limits in our ability to to observe, see, and measure what matters

insights.claim: Rives believes an information-theoretic model of the cell — treating the cell as an information-processing machine whose genome encodes the programs of life — is attainable via AI within roughly the next five years, while a full 'world model of life' down to atomic resolution remains very far off.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Sets a ~5-year horizon for credible general cell models; calibrate timelines for AI-native drug discovery accordingly.

insights.claim: The first practical target is a learned probabilistic transition function: given a cell or tissue state plus a set of inputs, predict a distribution of possible next cell states rather than a deterministic outcome.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Perturbation-response datasets (state + intervention -> outcome) are the key training asset; companies generating them at scale hold strategic data.
insights.quote: It's not going to be deterministic. You know, the cell the cell is going to transition, I think, to a distribution of of possible downstream states.

insights.claim: Rives says the intended data will link genetic, transcriptomic, protein-level and epigenetic readouts with imaging of how cells respond, so self-supervised pre-training can recover the latent variables driving input-output relationships.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Multi-modal linked datasets (omics + imaging) are the scarce input; watch spatial-omics and imaging vendors for demand pull.

insights.claim: Rives frames disease as part of the cell's program that often unfolds in very regular ways, so understanding those programs could yield fundamentally new tools to detect and intervene.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Underpins the case for programmable medicines beyond small-molecule pills.

insights.claim: Biohub's ambition is to move beyond the current therapeutic paradigm of pills and molecules toward far more programmable medicines that can 'read and write the programs of biology'.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Long-run tailwind for gene/cell/programmable therapeutic modalities over traditional small molecules.

insights.claim: The end-use of a cell-state model is to ask how to intervene to push a pathological cell state back into a healthy one, a question Rives expects the field to start tackling within five years.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: If realized, target discovery and reversal-of-state screening becomes model-driven; relevant to AI drug discovery platforms.

insights.claim: Biohub announced a $1.8 billion expansion of its Virtual Biology Initiative, a flagship data-generation partnership with the Department of Energy, the NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Big tech (Alphabet via DeepMind/Isomorphic, Meta) is co-funding public bio data; signals strategic interest in bio foundation models and could commoditize some proprietary cell data.

insights.claim: The Virtual Biology Initiative, first announced in April, aims to build datasets for a universal or general model of cellular biology and is inviting worldwide scientists and other funders to join.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Open, coordinated data generation may erode moats of startups whose edge is proprietary single-cell data.

insights.claim: A clear output of the initiative will be dramatically expanded contextual maps of cellular biology, especially spatial biology linking molecular measurements to imaging across hundreds of billions or more cells.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Large demand signal for spatial-omics and high-throughput imaging platforms and reagents.
insights.quote: be able to link molecular level measurements to imaging, and and really be able to do that at the scale of hundreds of billions or more cells

insights.claim: Rives expects first drafts of cell atlases distinguishing health from disease within 1-2 years and a fairly comprehensive map within five years given a focused, coordinated effort.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Timeline marker for when bio foundation models get usable disease-state training data.

insights.claim: Rives says health-vs-disease cell atlases should reveal both what makes each disease unique and shared common causes across different classes of disease.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Shared mechanisms could enable drug repurposing and platform therapies spanning multiple indications.

insights.claim: Rives argues such atlases would be enormously valuable even for classical non-AI analysis, and predicts much analysis of these datasets will be agentic in future.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Agentic analysis tooling for large bio datasets is an emerging category.

themes.theme: Measurement tech: laser phase plate and imaging

insights.claim: Biohub's laser phase plate — conceived by Holger Müller at Berkeley decades ago and funded by Biohub for years — is described as the world's most powerful standing-wave laser, interfering with the electron beam to give phase contrast in electron microscopy.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: A potential step change for cryo-EM instrumentation; watch for commercialization/licensing affecting electron microscope makers.
insights.quote: So So basically it's it's the most powerful standing wave laser in the world.

insights.claim: The laser phase plate's main application is cryo-electron tomography, where added contrast lets researchers distinguish individual proteins and macromolecules and their interactions inside the native cell despite extremely noisy observations.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Opens in-situ structural biology as a new data modality for models and drug discovery.

insights.claim: The laser phase plate only gives an atomic-resolution view of part of a cell, so Biohub's imaging institute is building complementary tools at each scale: cell-field perturbation imaging and whole-organism imaging.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: No single modality solves biology; portfolio approaches to data acquisition will dominate.

insights.claim: Biohub's data strategy targets four axes: more parameters measured per cell, more cells observed simultaneously, the temporal dimension over time, and the molecular dimension inside cells.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Useful checklist for evaluating life-science tools companies: which axis do they push?

insights.claim: Using transparent zebrafish, Biohub microscopes can track every single cell of a developing embryo from one cell to a full organism, and follow labeled immune cells as they move and interact in a living fish.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Whole-organism dynamic imaging is a differentiated dataset for developmental and immune modeling.

insights.claim: Rives notes ESM and AlphaFold did not come from training only on human proteins but on proteins across all of evolution, and training on human proteins alone would not yield an accurate predictive model.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Supports the value of cross-species datasets; non-human data is an asset, not a weakness, for bio foundation models.
insights.quote: If you train a model just on the human proteins you know you wouldn't you wouldn't get an accurate predictive model.

insights.claim: Rives argues core molecular machinery such as transcription factors and their interactions with enhancers and promoters is conserved across vertebrates while programs are rewired, so a predictive model integrating many species beats trying to build a perfect experimental proxy.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'works in mice' translation problem: AI that learns across species could improve preclinical-to-clinical translation.

insights.claim: Over-reliance on model organisms cuts both ways: false cures that only work in mice, and missed human-relevant mechanisms lacking a mouse proxy; organoids are the latest step toward better human proxies.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Organoid and human-relevant preclinical platforms remain a growing need despite AI.

themes.theme: LLM training recipe applied to biology

insights.claim: Rives expects biology to follow the same AI principles as other domains: self-supervised pre-training to learn the underlying system from statistical patterns, then an elicitation stage that brings out task-relevant capabilities.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Bio foundation model companies can borrow LLM playbooks; scale of pre-training data is a core moat.

insights.claim: Rives envisions RLVR for biology where verification happens in the laboratory, since unlike math or code biology cannot be verified quickly computationally.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Automated/closed-loop wet labs become the critical infrastructure for biology RL — a picks-and-shovels angle.
insights.quote: With biology, you know, we're going to have to build the systems that actually, you know, allow us allow verification in the laboratory.

insights.claim: The goal is 'empirical AI' — systems that ask a question, run the experiment, learn, and propose a better experiment in a recursive improvement loop.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Self-driving labs and AI-scientist platforms are the endgame architecture to watch.

insights.claim: Rives says the things we most want to know about biology are not in text and cannot be derived from first principles, so they require experiments, making predictive biology models critical alongside language-model reasoning.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Pure-LLM 'AI scientist' plays are insufficient for biology; proprietary experimental data and models retain value.
insights.quote: the things that we most want to know about biology they're not represented in text.

insights.claim: Rives is unsure whether language and biology models will fuse into one latent space; he sees it as hard initially due to scarce bridging data but probably achievable eventually.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Paired text-biology data is a scarce asset; whoever builds it could enable fused bio-language models.

insights.claim: Protein language models learn features representing the vast unknown protein biology — billions of proteins have been sequenced but the function of most is unknown — effectively novel concepts we have no words for.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Latent features of bio models may themselves be a discovery engine for novel function/targets.

insights.claim: Rives worries that modeling patient health records without a causal biological basis will mainly learn correlations that can't be linked back to deeper causal factors.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: EHR-centric AI may improve care delivery but is unlikely to produce step-change therapeutics.

insights.claim: Rives grants that health-record approaches could deliver real gains in matching existing drugs and mechanisms to the right patients and finding new patients who could benefit from existing drugs.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Near-term commercial value of EHR AI lies in patient matching and repurposing, not novel biology.

insights.claim: Rives views dense longitudinal human data (the host's 'million Bryan Johnsons' idea) as immensely valuable and likely to converge with cellular data over time, driven by continuous-monitoring technologies measuring more molecular parameters, but Biohub positions itself at the technology layer.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Continuous molecular monitoring devices are a potential long-term bridge between consumer health data and cell models.

insights.claim: Despite leading Biohub science, Rives says he barely tracks his own health beyond a sleep-tracking watch, with no regular blood tests.
insights.speaker: Alex Rives (Biohub)
insights.so_what: Signal that top researchers see current consumer health tracking as low-value relative to fundamental data.
